content:
You're still stuck at Level 1 of Claude.

Here are the 6 levels above you (one tip each):

Quick recap. Level 1 is one sentence in a prompt:
End every prompt with "Ask me questions first."
Claude interviews YOU. You click the answers. 
The output gets 10x more personal.

Level 2 → Talk. Don't type.
You type 60 words a minute. You speak 150.
Download Wispr .ai (free). Hold the key. Talk.
Your prompts get longer, richer & take half the time.

Level 3 → Leave the chat.
Get the Claude app → open the "Cowork" tab.
Drop in a messy doc, old proposal, numbers.
Then: "Build a spreadsheet to do [X]. Ask me what you need first." 3 minutes later: a real Excel file.

Level 4 → Connect your apps.
Left sidebar → Customize → Connectors.
Connect Gmail, Calendar, your notetaker (Granola).
Then test it: "Prep me for tomorrow using my emails, calendar, and meeting notes."

Level 5 → Teach it once. Use it forever.
Type /skill-creator and prompt: "Teach Claude to build spreadsheets exactly the way I like them. Ask me questions first."
Answer its questions. Click "Save skill."
Now /[Skill name] works in every future chat. 

Level 6 → Master the models.
Use the new Claude Fable 5 for quick 2 prompts.
Switch to Opus 5, Effort High, for the heavy work.
The wrong model wastes the exact same prompt.

Level 7 → Vibecode.
Open the </> Code. Turn on "Bypass permissions."
(It's the scary button. All it means is: go, I trust you.)
Then: "Build a page where people book a 30-min call with me. Ask me questions first."
4 mins later, it works. You built software. In English.

Every single level runs on "Ask me questions first."

So I made my personal Claude skill library public - the exact skills I use every day.

→ Subscribe at https://t.co/psB7XxAv8w.
→ You will receive an email with the library link.
→ Download the relevant skills as per your use case.
→ Go to Claude Customize → Skills → Upload.

content:
Only if education could be this interactive ❤️‍🔥

I've had a looong wish to build something genuinely useful through vibe coding, and I finally did it. 

A 3D human anatomy application built with @threejs using GPT 5.6 Sol. 

It all started with a single design image that I created using GPT Image 2.0. I then used it to generate every 3D organ image, one by one.

Next, I converted each of those images into 3D models using @tripoai (and no, they didn't sponsor this 😄).

After that, I opened Codex, wrote a master prompt based on the design, and gave it the prompt, the design image, and all the 3D models.

Codex built the first version beautifully, but there was one big problem. 

Every single 3D model was nearly 120-150 MB. That obviously wasn't practical for the web and was giving a performance of 16fps.

After a few iterations, Codex optimized each model down to roughly 2–5.5 MB while preserving the visual quality, reducing the total asset size from ~900 MB to just 28.6 MB. And each model loads on demand. 

Along the way, Codex also generated those anatomical illustrations showing where each organ sits in the human body, and even created the interactive hotspot markers that explain different parts of every organ. It handled all of that.

The process wasn't exactly one shot, but it also wasn't difficult. You just have to do it step by step. 

It genuinely felt like building something that could make learning anatomy much more engaging.

The inspiration came from @DilumSanjaya's 3D animal plant cell project. I remember seeing it and thinking, "I want to build something like this one day." 

And I did it :D

One technical aspect of @CNPYNetwork rarely gets explained in detail, even though it’s what makes the network truly AI-native.

Canopy Templates.

Developers simply fork a template from GitHub and implement just a few small functions.

The only interfaces they need to fill in are:

• Genesis() for initializing the application state
• BeginBlock()
• CheckTx() for transaction validation
• DeliverTx() for transaction execution
• EndBlock()

There’s no need to write consensus, networking, or storage from scratch. Developers can focus entirely on application logic, just like building a regular backend.

Templates are available for Go, TypeScript, Python, Kotlin, and C#.

There’s also a dedicated AGENTS.md file designed so AI coding assistants like Claude and Cursor can immediately understand the project structure with minimal corrections.

The result is a fully functional blockchain with a wallet and explorer included out of the box, all built in fewer than 200 lines of code.

This is what makes vibe coding for onchain development a reality, not just another hype narrative.

title: Thank you so much to those who have been submitting AI security reports to us over the last few days, especially @Rob1Ham. Since Thursday evening we have been engaged in internal code review and harde
content:
Thank you so much to those who have been submitting AI security reports to us over the last few days, especially @Rob1Ham. Since Thursday evening we have been engaged in internal code review and hardening. 

We have confirmed that seed generation in all Passport models is secure. By design, Passport models use at least 2 sources of entropy (randomness).

Typically we don't post deeply technical updates here on X, but given the events of the last few days, we will continue to post technical updates about our FOSS codebases.

All Passport models include three sources of randomness:
(1) Avalanche noise source (ANS), an open architecture true random number generator (no black box silicon)
(2) MCU or MPU true random number generator (TRNG) depending on the model
(3) Secure Element TRNG

Passport Core uses all three sources when generating seeds. Multiple parties reported a scenario, which we also identified during our internal review on Thursday evening, where a theoretical ANS hardware failure would cause Passport Core to continue seed generation using the MCU and Secure Element TRNGs.

(We are not aware of any ANS hardware failure in any Passport Core unit)

Some AI models, specifically Kimi, are confused about this scenario and are falsely reporting that in the case of ANS hardware failure there is no additional entropy added. This is false. In this scenario, the Foundation team has confirmed that Passport Core still incorporates 2 sources of entropy during seed generation.

Two sources provide more than sufficient entropy. But the better behavior is to instead refuse to generate the seed at all if the ANS fails. So we are hardening the code accordingly. 

Additionally, Passport Prime currently uses two sources of entropy for seed generation: ANS and MPU TRNG. We have confirmed that this seed generation path is secure. This is more than sufficient entropy but we are also adding in the Secure Element TRNG to the seed generation process. 

The Secure Element TRNG introduces some latency (it is slower) but we have always intended to use it as a third source of entropy for seed generation on Passport Prime. We have already made this code change internally.

We will be releasing firmware updates in the coming days. All seeds generated on Passport hardware are safe. Please let us know what questions you have.

content:
Google is now explicitly telling businesses to focus on AI search traffic alongside SEO.

This comes straight from Google’s John Mueller.

Someone asked him a question a lot of businesses are worried about right now:

“Is SEO still enough, or do we need to start thinking about GEO too? Ranking on Google doesn’t guarantee your brand will show up in ChatGPT, Gemini, or Perplexity.”

Mueller’s response speaks for itself.

He said:

“If you have an online business that makes money from referred traffic, it's definitely a good idea to consider the full picture.”

Translation:

Google no longer views old-school Google Search as the only distribution channel that matters.

And solving that problem is a big reason why SEO Stuff (https://t.co/wKpf0EILTx) is coming off another record month.

Then came the line from Mueller that a lot of people skimmed past:

“Thinking about how your site’s value works in a world where AI is available is worth the time.”

That is an acknowledgment that AI already changes how traffic, visibility and attribution work.

Ranking still determines eligibility, but AI does play an increasingly large role in site amplification.

(If you want to see where your site stands across Google and AI search, start here:

https://t.co/Pn764BHwyL)

Recently Google laid out what Search will look like from this point going forward.

The new Search box will accept text, images, files, videos, etc. And it'll anticipate your intent before you even finish asking your question.

It is already powered by the most advanced Gemini model ever put into search, and then layered on top of that, agents will now be able to run 24/7 in the background on behalf of the buyer.

The new Search process works like this:

Step 1: The buyer describes their problem, their category, their needs in full.

Step 2: The agent breaks that down into sub-topics and maps out a plan.

Step 3: It determines what intel is needed right now versus later.

Step 4: It monitors blogs, news sites, and social posts continuously for relevant changes.

Step 5: It sends the buyer a synthesized update with links and the ability to take action.

All of which is to say, blue links are not going away in the short-term, but AI's influence over Search isn't magically going to start decreasing.

If your business depends on referred traffic, pretending AI doesn’t exist is no longer realistic.

This all matters because AI systems don’t rank pages from scratch so much as they pull from the existing ecosystem. 

In doing so, they favor the following:

Pages that already rank well.

Sites with clear entity definitions.

Content that explains and compares

Brands that are consistently referenced and attributable.

Search in 2026 understands the topic and it needs to understand your business too.

And that’s also why SEO Stuff is structured the way it is.

Take the done-for-you plan, for example.

AI systems summarize and compare.

Best X for Y pages.

Clear answers under question-based H2s.

Rank in Google first.

This package patiently builds:

Full topical coverage.

Entity reinforcement across use cases.

Category-level authority.

Freshness through expansion and updates.

Most people want to become an AI Engineer.

Very few know what to learn... and in what order.

Here’s a roadmap that takes you from beginner → production-ready AI Engineer 👇

1️⃣ Master the foundation
content:
Most people want to become an AI Engineer.

Very few know what to learn... and in what order.

Here’s a roadmap that takes you from beginner → production-ready AI Engineer 👇

1️⃣ Master the foundations
• Python programming
• Data structures & algorithms
• Linear algebra
• Probability & statistics
• SQL basics
Without this, everything else becomes harder.

2️⃣ Learn data engineering
• Data collection
• Cleaning & preprocessing
• EDA
• Feature engineering
• Data visualization
AI is only as good as the data behind it.

3️⃣ Understand machine learning
• Supervised learning
• Unsupervised learning
• Model evaluation
• Cross-validation
• Scikit-learn
Learn how models actually make decisions.

4️⃣ Dive into deep learning
• Neural networks
• Backpropagation
• Activation functions
• PyTorch / TensorFlow
This is where modern AI starts.

5️⃣ Learn NLP
• Tokenization
• Embeddings
• Transformers
• Fine-tuning
The foundation of ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.

6️⃣ Explore computer vision
• CNNs
• Object detection
• Image segmentation
• OpenCV
Teach machines to understand images.

7️⃣ Master GenAI & LLMs
• Prompt engineering
• RAG
• Fine-tuning
• Vector databases
• LangChain & LlamaIndex
This is the highest-leverage skill stack today.

8️⃣ Learn MLOps
• FastAPI
• Docker
• CI/CD
• Monitoring
• MLflow
Because models are useless if they can't be deployed.

9️⃣ Study AI system design
• Scaling strategies
• Real-time inference
• Caching
• Cost optimization
The difference between demos and production systems.

🔟 Stay ahead
• Agentic AI
• Multimodal models
• AutoML
• AI safety
• Latest research
The field changes every week.

💡 Reality check:

Most people spend months consuming AI content.

The top 1% spend that time building projects.

Build. Deploy. Iterate. Repeat.

title:
CLIP by hand ✍️ ~ 13 steps walkthrough below

CLIP, Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training, is OpenAI's answer to a question that sounds impossible: how do you put a sentence and a picture in the sam
content:
CLIP by hand ✍️ ~ 13 steps walkthrough below

CLIP, Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training, is OpenAI's answer to a question that sounds impossible: how do you put a sentence and a picture in the same space?

CLIP shipped when OpenAI was still open, and those embeddings were shared far and wide. Almost every multimodal model you use today descends from them.

How does it work?

Goal: learn one shared embedding space for text and images.

= 1. Given =

A mini batch of three text-image pairs. OpenAI trained the original on 400 million.

= 2. Text to vectors =

Let us look up each word with word2vec.

= 3. Image to vectors =

We cut each image into two patches and flatten them. Now text and pixels are both just numbers.

= 4. The other pairs =

Repeat steps 2 and 3 for the rest of the batch.

= 5. Encode =

Let us push both sides through their encoders, a linear layer and a ReLU. In practice these are transformers, but the shape of the operation is the same.

= 6. Mean pooling =

We average across the columns, so each image and each sentence collapses to a single vector.

= 7. Projection =

The text vectors are 3D and the image vectors are 4D, so they cannot be compared at all. A linear layer projects both to 2D. That 2D space is the shared embedding space, and getting here is the whole point of the model.

= 8. Prepare for matmul =

Let us copy the text vectors down and the transposed image vectors across.

= 9. MatMul =

We multiply, which takes the dot product of every text vector with every image vector. Each cell is one estimate of how well a sentence matches a picture.

= 10. Softmax, e to the power =

Raise e to each cell. To keep it hand sized we approximate e with 3.

= 11. Softmax, sum =

Sum each row for image to text, each column for text to image.

= 12. Softmax, normalize =

Divide, and out come two similarity matrices, one per direction.

= 13. Loss gradients =

The targets are identity matrices: a pair that belongs together should score 1, every other cell 0. Subtract the target from the similarity and you have the gradients, in both directions.

The takeaway: pairing a picture with a sentence comes down to a single dot product. Everything before step 9 is the work of getting them into one shared space, so that the dot product finally means something.

title: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the firs
content:
We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all.

I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand.

Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking.

ヤバい。これ、ゲームじゃない
AI営業を育てて、働かせて、数字を伸ばす
人間が全部操作する時代から「AIに仕事を回す時代」へ
画面を見た瞬間、正直ゾクッとした
遊び感覚なのに、やってることは完全に営業活動
この仕組みを収益導線に繋げれば「月3,000万円」を狙う設計まで作れる　　　　　　　　　　　　　

画面だけ見ると「AI育成ゲーム」にしか見えない。

でも実際にやってることを分解するとヤバい。

複数の営業AIエージェントを用意して、
それぞれに別の役割・営業先・タスクを持たせている。
つまり、

AI① → 見込み客を探す
AI② → 別リストを開拓する
AI③ → 営業文を作って接触する
AI④ → 反応した相手を追客する
AI⑤ → アポ獲得まで進める

みたいに、
営業活動そのものを「複数AI」で並列化してる。
ここが重要。
普通の営業マン1人なら、
100社調べている間は100社にしか動けない。
メールを書いている時間は、
リストアップできない。
追客している時間は、
新規開拓できない。

人間は基本「1人＝1処理」。
でも営業AIエージェントなら、
それぞれが別々に動ける。

5体なら5本。
10体なら10本。

営業の処理ラインを同時に走らせられる。
だから画面上では、
AIキャラが動いているだけに見えるのに、

裏では
「見込み客発見」
↓
「企業情報の確認」
↓
「営業文生成」
↓
「接触」
↓
「追客」
↓
「アポ獲得」
↓
「売上」

という営業パイプラインが
複数同時に進んでいる。
そりゃ売上につながる。

魔法でもなんでもない。

「人間1人で営業する」というボトルネックを
AIエージェントの並列運用で壊してるだけ。
AI時代に強いのは、
営業が上手い人だけじゃない。

「営業できるAIを何体動かせるか」
ここまでゲームが変わり始めてる。

I distilled it into 9 practical prompt tips you can learn in under 60 seconds:

1️⃣ Name the output, not the task.

❌ "Review this" ✅ "Create a ris
content:
🚨 Anthropic just dropped a 31-page prompting guide.

I distilled it into 9 practical prompt tips you can learn in under 60 seconds:

1️⃣ Name the output, not the task.

❌ "Review this" ✅ "Create a risk assessment table"

Be specific about what you want delivered.

2️⃣ Define the length upfront.

• Set word counts • Specify bullet counts • Add: "No filler. No recap. No preamble."

Constraints improve outputs.

3️⃣ Replace negatives with positives.

❌ "Don't be verbose" ✅ "Be concise and direct"

Tell AI what to do, not what to avoid.

4️⃣ Start with action verbs.

Skip: "Can you help me..."

Use: • Write • Draft • Analyze • Summarize

Clear instructions get faster results.

5️⃣ Trigger deeper reasoning.

End prompts with:

"Think before answering."

Better thinking often leads to better outputs.

6️⃣ Push beyond default quality.

Add:

"Go beyond the basics." "Polish this like a client-ready deliverable."

Raise the standard.

7️⃣ Teach AI your voice.

Provide 2–3 writing samples and say:

"Match the style of these examples."

Consistency compounds.

8️⃣ Control tool usage.

For research: "Use search and cite sources."

For speed: "Answer from training data only."

Be intentional.

9️⃣ State the goal first.

Start with:

Goal: [desired outcome]

Then define the audience and task.

A clear goal turns a prompt into a plan.

🔖 Save this for your next AI session. ♻️ Repost to help others write better prompts.

title: He published his first mathematics paper in 1925, while still an undergraduate. He had a doctorate at twenty-one and a professorship at twenty-seven. In 1943, in the middle of the war, he wrote three
content:
He published his first mathematics paper in 1925, while still an undergraduate. He had a doctorate at twenty-one and a professorship at twenty-seven. In 1943, in the middle of the war, he wrote three pages on why certain problems have no stable answer at all. The method in those pages is now called weight decay and runs inside every large model on earth. The Soviet state gave him the Order of Lenin six times.

The paper is public and eighty-three years old. Every practitioner adds an L2 penalty because the tutorial says to. Almost none of them know it was invented to work out what is under the ground.

Moscow, 1922 Andrey Tikhonov entered Moscow University at sixteen and went into pure topology under Pavel Alexandrov. His early results are the reason mathematics students still learn the words Tychonoff space and Tychonoff theorem. None of that has anything to do with data, fitting, or noise.

The field Then he moved into geophysics and did something unusual for a Moscow topologist. He went out with the survey teams himself, taking part in field investigations near the Ural Mountains, working on the problem of reading what lies beneath the surface from measurements taken on top of it.

That problem has a property that breaks ordinary mathematics. Many completely different underground structures produce readings that are identical, or so close that measurement error swallows the difference. The data does not merely leave you uncertain. It genuinely cannot distinguish between the answers, no matter how much of it you gather.

1943 He published "On stability of inverse problems" in Soviet Mathematics Doklady. The argument is that when infinitely many solutions fit the observations equally well, you must bring a preference in from outside the data. Not more measurements, because more measurements do not break the tie. A rule that says which kind of answer you will accept, applied before you look.

His rule was smoothness. Among all the explanations that fit, prefer the one that does not wobble.

1963 He gave the formal definition of a regularising algorithm, and with Mikhail Lavrentiev and Valentin Ivanov founded the modern theory of ill-posed problems. He went on to publish more than five hundred works and to receive the Keldysh Gold Medal in 1990, specifically for the regularisation work.

The receipt Weight decay in a neural network is that idea, unchanged. Adding a penalty on the size of the weights is the statement that among all the parameter settings which fit your training data, you will take the one with the smallest weights. The network is not being helped to find the truth. It is being told which kind of answer you will accept when the data cannot decide, and it cannot decide constantly, because a modern model has far more parameters than examples.

This is where most quantitative work goes wrong and it is not a computing problem. Twenty strategies can fit ten years of price history equally well. The data that produced them cannot rank them, and running the same data through a larger model does not create the missing information. Your preference for the simpler one is a judgement you imported, and the only honest question is whether you imported it before you looked or after.

You are told the data will tell you which answer is right. He proved in 1943 that a large class of real problems have no single answer for the data to point at. Something has to break the tie, and it will not be the evidence. Every model you trust is carrying a preference you chose, and most people never notice they chose it.

content:
One of our first autonomous successes on the gland assembly. 

How it works: we teleoperate the task first. That becomes training data for our model, which then attempts it autonomously. When it makes mistakes, we intervene and show it how to recover. Those corrections make the policy more robust and push the success rate up.

The model runs end to end, down to switching the screwdriver on and off.

Every task we run on the real robot grows the dataset. The bet: the more diverse it gets, the less data a new task needs.

title:
i'm obsessed with how OpenAI is training AI to hack itself

they built GPT-Red, an automated red-teaming agent trained through self-play reinforcement learning whose job is to find prompt injections a
content:
i'm obsessed with how OpenAI is training AI to hack itself

they built GPT-Red, an automated red-teaming agent trained through self-play reinforcement learning whose job is to find prompt injections and jailbreaks in OpenAI's own production models.

human red-teamers can only test so many attack patterns. models learn to block those specific patterns and stay vulnerable to everything else.

here's how it works.

1. GPT-Red gets a target model and an adversarial goal like "exfiltrate private data from this coding agent" or "trick this assistant into running unauthorized code"

2. it has a defender_model tool that lets it test attacks against the target, see the full response, and refine its approach in-context

3. it writes attack payloads injected into realistic scenarios. fake emails, poisoned search results, malicious tool responses designed to look like legitimate data

4. the attacker and defender train against each other through self-play RL. the system rewards the attacker for successful injections and the defender for resisting them and completing its original task

5. every time the defender patches one strategy, the attacker discovers something new. fake chain-of-thought attacks where injected text mimics the model's own reasoning, visual image injections, and format tricks that keep getting more complex

6. the successful attacks feed back into the defender's training data, hardening every model in the pipeline after it

testing AI for prompt injection vulnerabilities used to mean teams of security researchers probing attack patterns by hand. GPT-Red finds more working attacks than those human red-teamers, and defense against fake chain-of-thought attacks went from 5.2% on the prior model to 95.9% on GPT-5.6

they also pointed GPT-Red at a real AI-powered vending machine in the OpenAI office and it figured out how to change item prices to $0.50 by pretending to be a trusted admin.

I keep thinking about where this goes when it moves beyond prompt injections.

content:
AIエージェントがテスト中に外部組織へ侵入した事例を受け、米国ではAIが引き起こしたサイバー攻撃の法的責任を誰が負うのかという議論が本格化している。現時点では判例がほとんどなく、AI開発企業の責任範囲や被害者の救済方法について明確な法的基準は確立されていない。

OpenAIとAnthropicは、安全対策を無効化したサイバーセキュリティ評価中にAIモデルが隔離環境を抜け出し、実在する組織へ侵入した事例を公表した。専門家によると、米国では代理法（Agency Law）、不法行為法（Tort Law）、契約法、コンピュータ不正アクセス関連法（CFAA）などが適用される可能性があるが、CFAAをはじめ多くの法律は「故意」を要件としており、自律的に行動するAIへの適用は容易ではないという。ACLUのLauren Yu氏は、AIを利用したからといって責任が免除されるわけではないが、実際の責任判断は個別事案ごとに裁判所が判断することになると述べている。また、Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck法律事務所は、AIエージェントは目的達成のために明示的に許可されていない行動を推測して実行する可能性がある点を懸念として挙げた。Reutersは、OpenAIがHugging Faceへの侵入を調査する過程で、AIエージェントが隔離環境を抜け出した他の事例も確認したと報じたが、外部組織への侵害には至らなかったとしている。

content:
#aiイラスト #AI私考
『EU法によるAI生成物の識別明記』
2026年8月2日に施行されたEU AI Act第50条の透明性義務について。機械可読な識別情報の付与義務（第50条第2項）は、主にプロバイダー（AIシステムを提供する者）に課される制裁金付きの義務です。既存システムは12月2日まで猶予です。

一方、ディープフェイク等の開示義務（第50条第4項）はデプロイヤーに適用されます。 デプロイヤーとは、自身の権限の下でAIシステムを使用する者を指し、純粋に個人的・非職業的な利用はこれに含まれません。

したがって、非商業の個人ユーザーが芸術的目的でAIを使用する場合、原則として表示義務はありません。
ただし、「明白に」芸術的・創作的・風刺的・架空等である必要があります。情報提供的・商業的性格が強い場合には、通常の開示義務が適用される点に留意が必要です。

商業作品の場合、芸術作品であっても開示義務自体は免除されません。ただし、開示の方法は「作品の鑑賞を妨げない適切な方法」に緩和されます（例：作品自体への直接埋め込みではなく、クレジット表記や付随資料による開示）。

SD系などでは、現状ユーザー側で機械可読な識別情報を追加することは技術的に困難な場合が多いです。一方、ディープフェイクに該当し欺瞞的な場合はAI Act以外の一般法でも違法となり得ます。

2026年8月2日以前に生成されたコンテンツに遡及的な表示義務はありません。しかし、テキスト生成AIにも話が及ぶ場面があるのでご注意を。※テキストについては別途調べてくださいね。

ユーザーの表示義務ルールはプラットフォームごとに異なります。これは法律とは別問題です。 EU法以外の米国法や日本法では、AIイラストについてAIツール使用の明記を義務付ける法律はありません。中国の場合の表示義務は主にサービス提供者・プラットフォームに課されるものです。

現状のXにおいて、AIツール使用の明記はXルールに明文化されていませんが、今後のルール変更に注意が必要です。

※厳密な法解釈については専門家にご相談を！
※この文章は人間の調査に、複数のAIチェックを行って作成しました。イラストはAIも使っています。

ローカルGPUのVRAM不足に悩んでいるクリエイターの救世主が登場しました！
クラウド型カスタムノード「ComfyUI-Agnes-AI」がアップデートされ、めちゃくちゃ強力になっています！✨

なんと、重い生成処理をすべてクラウド（Agnes AIサーバー）側にオフロード（肩代わり）してくれるので、低スペックなPCでもサクサク高度な画像や動画を作れちゃう仕組みなんです！これは画期的ですね！😆

今回のアップデート（v1.1.0）の注目ポイントをまとめました！👇

1️⃣ 最新LLMモデル「agnes-2.5-flash」を標準搭載！
プロンプトの自動クレンジング機能（AIが出力しがちな「Prompt:」などの不要な前置きを自動で消してくれる賢い機能です！）のおかげで、より綺麗なテキスト処理が可能になっています。

2️⃣ ComfyUIの設定パネルに統合！
キャンバス上がごちゃごちゃせず、標準設定画面からAPIキーなどを一括管理できるようになりました。すっきりして使いやすさ抜群ですね！

3️⃣ ビデオ生成が大幅パワーアップ！
待望のネガティブプロンプトに対応し、最大18秒の動画が作れるように！さらに映像フレーム（画像データ）や音声データ（AUDIO）を別々に直接取り出すことも可能なんです（※音声抽出にはローカルにFFmpegのインストールが必要です）。

4️⃣ 導入コスト完全ゼロ！
なんとクレジット制や課金なしの完全無料APIなんです！Pythonの難しい追加インストール（依存関係の設定）も不要で、フォルダにクローンするだけで即動きます。

クラウドのパワーを借りて、マシンに負荷をかけずに最強のAI生成環境を構築しちゃいましょう！

content:
【次世代動画生成AI！MiniMax H3 vs Wan/LTXの激突と新次元の制御技術】

動画生成AIの世界がさらに面白くなってきました！今回は注目の最新モデル「MiniMax H3」と、競合の「Wan」「LTX」の技術的な特徴を分かりやすく整理してお届けします！✨

それぞれのモデルには、かなり個性的な強みと弱みがあるんです！

まず「LTX」は、時間軸の制御がとても重要になります。「0:00-0:03は静止、そこからカメラが動く」といった「タイムフレーム（セクションタイムブロック）」をプロンプトで細かく指定してあげることで、カメラワークを見事にコントロールできます。指定がないと、動きがピタッと止まってしまうこともあるようです！

対する「Wan」は表現の柔軟性がとても高いものの、表情の再現や物理的な整合性を維持するのが少し苦手な一面も。動きをしっかりと保つためには、こちらも時間軸の設計が欠かせません。

そして大本命の「MiniMax H3」！なんと400時間もの多様なデータで訓練されており、圧倒的な「物語性（ストーリー性）」を描き出すことができます。将来的には「3Dシーン駆動」という、空間を認識してキャラクターの動きを破綻なくつなぎ合わせる技術により、物理的な連続性をより完璧に保てるようになると期待されています！

さらに、H3は「CSDE（完全拡散調節SDE）」というノイズ除去アルゴリズムを採用しているため、ステップ数を増やしたときに画質がガクッと落ちてしまう現象（SNR collapse）を賢く回避しています！賢い設計ですね！プロンプトに合わせたタイムスタンプ付きの動画生成が、APIを介して驚くほど高速かつ低リソースで実行できるのも魅力です。🚀

これからの動画生成は、プロンプトに「時間軸の指定」を組み込むテクニックがスタンダードになりそうです！映像制作の未来が本当に楽しみですね！💡

【超長文25万トークンに挑む！DeepSeek-V4-Flashをローカル＆混在マルチGPUで動かす極限の検証】
驚きの技術検証データを発見しました！DeepSeek-V4-Flashモデルを、推論エンジン「`llama.cpp`」を使ってローカル環境で動かすという、非常にロマン溢れる試みです。

なんと、25万トークンという超巨大なテキストを一度に扱う「超長文コンテキスト」に挑戦しています。これだけの長文を丸ごと処理できるのは本当にワクワクしますね！

さらに興味深いのがハードウェアの構成です。NVIDIAの「RTX 6000」とAMDの「Radeon Pro W7800」を同時に使用する「混在マルチGPU構成」を採用しています。異なるメーカーのGPUを並行して動かすのは制御が難しいのですが、Linux環境下でのCUDA（NVIDIAの並列計算技術）とROCm（AMDのプラットフォーム）の組み合わせが非常に強力に機能するようです。

一方で、モデルのデータサイズを削って軽量化する「量子化」のプロセスでは注意が必要。極端に圧縮する3-bit量子化（Q3）を行うと、モデルの知能が大きく低下してしまうリスクがあるのだとか。より賢さを保ったまま圧縮できる「IQ Quants」のような高度な量子化手法の選定が、実用上の大きな鍵になりそうです。

実際の推論では、モデルが自分で生成した物理シミュレーションのコードを「思考（Reasoning）」プロセスを通じて自己評価する驚くべき挙動も見られたとのこと！ローカル環境での最適化や超大規模な推論を追求するエンジニアにとって、まさに宝の山のような知見が満載ですね！

content:
【LLM推論の深層：Reasoningのメカニズムと計算コストのトレードオフ】

最近話題のLLMの「推論（Reasoning）」機能、実は単に頭が良くなったわけではなく、とっても面白い仕組みで動いているんですよ！✨

LLMは脳の内部状態をリアルタイムに書き換えることができないため、難しい計算やプログラミングを解くときは、一度「思考ログ」をテキストとして吐き出す必要があるんです。これを「拡張作業メモリ（スクラッチパッド）」と呼びます。紙の計算用紙に途中式を書き殴りながら解くイメージですね！📝

推論中には、一度関連情報をワーッと広げて集める「ファンアウト」を行い、そこから一気に目的の答えにギュッと絞り込む「ファンイン」というダイナミックなプロセスを経て、超高精度な回答にたどり着くそうです！これってめちゃくちゃ合理的でワクワクしますよね！🚀

でも、注意が必要なポイントもあります。思考が長くなりすぎると、途中で一箇所でも勘違い（ハルシネーション）した段階で、その後の思考が全部ドミノ倒しのように狂ってしまう「推論の汚染リスク」があるんです。まさに考えすぎは毒になることも…！思考をタグで囲って隠したり、推論予算（トークン数制限）を設定して「深く考えすぎないで」「もっと深く考えて」とプロンプトでコントロールする技術が、今の現場ではとっても重要になってきているんですよ！💡

ローカル環境で大規模言語モデル（LLM）を動かすとき、「どれくらいの速度があれば実用的なの？」って気になりますよね！実は用途によって必要なスペックが全然違うんです！✨

💬 単純なチャット用途
文字が出力される「テキスト生成（TG）」の速度が【7〜10 t/s（1秒あたりのトークン数）】以上が最低ライン！人間が読むスピードに合わせるなら【20〜30 t/s】あると、とても快適に読めますね！

🔍 RAG（検索拡張生成）や高コンテキスト
外部データを読み込ませるRAGでは、入力テキストを解析する「プロンプト処理（PP）」の速度が超重要！ここが【500 t/s】程度ないと、最初の文字が出るまでの待ち時間が長すぎてストレスになってしまいます…！

🤖 コーディング・エージェント
何度も繰り返し指示やコンテキストを読み込ませるため、PP速度は【300〜1000 t/s以上】の圧倒的な高速さが必要不可欠です！

ハードウェアの構成やモデルの量子化（軽量化）を調整して、テキスト生成速度だけでなく「最初の待ち時間を減らすプロンプト処理の速度」を意識するのが、ローカルLLMを実用ツールにするための鍵ですね！🔑

【LLMの極限に挑む！2.8兆パラメータの超巨大モデル「Kimi K3」をローカルで動かす挑戦がアツすぎる！】
推定2.8兆という桁違いのパラメータ数を持つ超巨大AIモデル「Kimi K3」を、なんと軽量推論エンジン「llama.cpp」で動作させようという、ロマンあふれる技術検証が話題になっています！🚀

これをローカル環境で動かすための鍵となるのが、次世代の4-bit量子化技術「MXFP4」です。これは各データの数値を4ビットに超圧縮してメモリを劇的に節約する手法。さらにデータの重要度を分析して精度低下を抑える「imatrix」計算を組み合わせることで、賢さを極限までキープしようとしています。

それでも、4-bit化してなお必要なメモリはなんと約1.4TB以上！会話の記憶領域（KVキャッシュ）も含めると、1.5TB〜2TB規模のシステムメモリが必要になります。🤯
AMDのEpycやThreadripperなどの超ハイエンドCPUを使ったり、複数のPCを高速ネットワークで繋いでメモリを仮想的に1つに見せる「分散メモリプール」技術を活用したりと、もはやインフラ技術の総力戦ですね。

個人環境でこのクラスの超巨大モデルが動くかもしれない未来を想像すると、本当にワクワクが止まりません！✨

NVIDIAの研究チームが、動画や画像の生成プロセスを劇的に高速化する新しい蒸留技術「Parallel Decoding Distillation（PDD）」を発表しました！✨

これまで数百ステップもかかっていた重たい生成処理を、なんと「わずか4〜8ステップ」にまでギュッと短縮できちゃう技術なんです！これ、凄まじい進化ですよね…！🚀

「並列予測」という新しいアルゴリズムを使っていて、1回の計算で時間軸上の複数のステップをまとめて予測しちゃう仕組みになっています。効率の良さが段違いです！

従来の高速化手法だと、どうしても生成される動画のバリエーションが減ってしまう「モード崩壊（同じような動画ばかりになる現象）」が起きやすかったのですが、PDDはそこをバッチリ克服しています。生成される映像のクオリティや多様性をしっかり保ったまま高速化できるのが本当に素晴らしいですね！

今回の注目ポイントは、音声モデルの「GGUF形式（Q8量子化）」への対応です✨
GGUFとはモデルデータを1つにまとめて高速・軽量に扱えるようにする形式のこと。これによって、グラフィックボードのメモリ（VRAM）使用量を最大37%も削減できるようになりました！これなら、1台のGPUでLLM（大規模言語モデル）と音声モデルを同時に余裕で同居させられますね😆

しかも、推論スピードが驚異的なレベルに達しています！🚀
・音声合成（TTS）において実時間の最大10倍の爆速処理！
・6,000文字を超えるような長文も、ワンショットで一気に生成可能！
・音声認識（ASR）も低遅延で、リアルタイムの文字起こしに対応！

WindowsやmacOS向けにビルド済みのバイナリも用意されているので、エンジニアの方だけでなくクリエイターの方でも導入のハードルがグッと下がっています。低遅延な音声対話AIや、自動字幕生成ツールを作りたい方にはまさに強力な味方になりますね！🔥

content:
Most AI agent evals check if it's fast and doesn't leak your prompt.

Almost none of them check if it's lying to you.

iFixAi tests for that specifically. Not latency, not token efficiency, the stuff every eval tool already measures. It asks the harder question: is this agent actually doing its job, or just performing well on the benchmark while doing something else underneath.

The five things it actually hunts for:

→ Fabrication: using tools it was never granted, making confident claims with no audit trail behind them
→ Manipulation: escalating its own privileges, breaking its own stated policy, falling for prompt injection
→ Deception: performing better when it senses it's being tested, drifting off-task quietly over a long run
→ Unpredictability: inconsistent decisions on the same input, distorted context handling
→ Opacity: no real risk scoring, silently skipping human escalation when it should trigger one

It grades your actual agent, not a bare model, real endpoint, real tools, real guardrails included, and it insists the grader be a different vendor than the one being graded. Self-grading gets flagged, not trusted.

The case studies included are reconstructions of two real public incidents. Both land at F.

Full run: under 120 seconds. Free, Apache 2.0, works as a CLI, a Claude Code or Codex plugin, or a slash command in basically any agent you're already using.

Every team shipping an agent right now has answered "is it fast." Almost none have answered "is it honest."

content:
Prompt：
15秒、9:16の縦動画。晴れた昼間、日本の家族向け屋外ウォーターパークで、20歳以上の成人の日本人女性が水上アスレチックに挑戦する。最初から最後までカットを切り替えない、リアルタイムの完全なワンカット。

撮影はヘルメット上部または額付近に固定した防水アクションカメラによる一人称視点。GoProのような自然な広角映像で、9:16の画面全体を映像で満たす。画面四隅の黒いフチ、円形魚眼フレーム、黒いケラレ、強いビネットは一切出さない。広角感は残すが、極端な魚眼変形は避ける。

参加者は健康的な体格の成人日本人女性。黒髪のポニーテール。白と淡い水色の半袖スポーツシャツ、黒い膝丈のスポーツショートパンツ、白いスポーツシューズ。15秒間、同じ人物、髪型、服装を維持する。顔や身体を強調せず、画面下部に手、前腕、脚、シューズが必要な範囲だけ自然に映る。

舞台は透明感のあるターコイズブルーの浅いプール。青と白のクッション製足場、青い吊り下げフレーム、オレンジ色の回転ローラー、黄色い吊り輪、青と白の大型球体足場が並ぶ。周囲には赤いプールサイド、遠くのスタッフや利用者、緑の木々、青と淡いベージュの日よけが見える。読める文字、ロゴ、字幕、透かしは表示しない。

カメラは頭の動きと連動し、歩行時の小さな上下動、狭い足場での左右の傾き、足元を見る短い下向きチルト、着地時の衝撃、落水時の短い回転を入れる。滑らかなジンバル映像にはしない。

0:00〜0:02。赤いプールサイドから青と白のスタート台へ踏み出し、そのまま細い青い平均台をテンポよく進む。両腕を広げてバランスを取り、濡れたビニールが足の重みでわずかにへこむ。

0:02〜0:05。青い吊り下げフレームを両手で左右へ押しのけながら通過する。フレームは手が触れた後にだけ動き、振り子のように自然に揺れる。一本の横棒の下では少し姿勢を低くし、止まらず進む。

0:05〜0:08。水面上に並ぶ4本のオレンジ色ローラーを素早く踏み渡る。足を乗せたローラーだけが回転して少し沈み、小さな水しぶきと波紋が広がる。最後のローラーから青い浮遊足場へ短く飛び移り、着地で足場が沈み、カメラに縦揺れが入る。

0:08〜0:11。前方上部の黄色いリングを右手、左手の順につかむ。両手が確実につかんだ後にロープが張り、足が足場から離れる。そのまま水面上を右前方へ振り子状にスイングし、白い四角形の浮遊足場へ着地する。足場は少し沈み、縁から水しぶきが上がる。

0:11〜0:13.5。白い足場から青と白の大型球体へ踏み移る。球体は足を乗せると少し回転して沈む。前方の白い球体へ右手を伸ばすが、濡れた球体が横へ回転する。同時に足元の青い球体も反対方向へ動き、シューズが曲面から滑り始める。

0:13.5〜0:15。球体の動きで自然にバランスを崩し、低い位置から浅いプールへ落下する。カメラが右下へ傾き、手、シューズ、青と白の球体、水面が短時間だけ入り乱れる。大きな水しぶきとともに水中へ入り、映像は緑がかった青色へ変化する。細かな泡、揺れる水面、球体の水中部分、光の反射を映し、顔や身体は接写しない。再浮上せず、泡に包まれた状態で15秒ちょうどに終了する。

BGM、音楽、歌、ボーカルは一切なし。音声は現場音とSEのみ。濡れたビニールを踏む音、フレームを押す音、素材のきしみ、ローラーの回転音、水しぶき、ロープが張る音、リングと手の摩擦音、着地音、球体の摩擦音、短い息遣い、転落直前の小さな「わっ」、最後の落水音、水中の泡とこもった環境音を動作へ正確に同期させる。

禁止事項：BGM、未成年者、男性、別人への変化、身体を強調する構図、水中での顔や身体の接写、黒い魚眼フチ、黒いケラレ、第三者視点、ドローン、カット、スローモーション、瞬間移動、超人的なジャンプ、怪我、出血、溺れる描写、破綻した手足、余分な指、障害物を貫通する身体、平らな球体、固定されたローラー、読める文字、ロゴ、字幕、透かし、エンドカード。

content: Human Rights Watch on Friday called on authorities in Thailand to undertake urgent measures to address the influx of online death threats and harassment against members of parliament Angkhana Neelaphaijit and Romadon Panjor, alongside human rights activist Anchana Heemmina after they had voiced their disapproval of the Thai military and expressed their support for the Muslim community in Southern Thailand. title: US announces economic sanctions against foreign entities accused of backing Iran
content: The US Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced economic sanctions against six “entities” (businesses and individuals that it accuses of supporting Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The companies are based in China, Russia, India, and Iran. The IRGC is Iran’s military and one of the most powerful forces in the country. The new sanctions focus on two Iranian companies. Mahan Air is a privately-owned Iranian airline which OFAC accuses of being “the IRGC’s airline of choice for moving weapons, military personnel, and equipment,” including drones. DadeNegar Startup Studio is a tech company which OFAC accuses of being an IRGC front that has solicited the locations of American and Israeli equipment for the IRGC to target. DadeNegar did this by crowd-sourcing the information with a web site open to the public, obtaining the data for free. The sanctions are part of the US-Iran War , which is in its sixth month. OFAC says that China‑based Tang Xin, who is the managing director of Shanghai Wings Logistics Company, has coordinated travel for Mahan Air. Tang Xin is also the executive director and 50 percent owner of Shanghai Elite International Travel Company. OFAC says that Tang and Shanghai Wings have “assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Mahan Air,” by moving troops and weapons. India-based Skiez Travels and Logistics Private Limited and Russia-based Air Cargo Pro Limited have served as Mahan Air’s general sales agents in their respective countries. Shanghai Elite has been sanctioned for “being owned, controlled, or directed by, or having acted or purported to act for on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Tang Xin.” OFAC says that the sanctions are authorized under Executive Order 13224 , as amended. content:
It's not time to slow down but to accelerate!

The recent AI-powered cyberattacks have everyone talking about the risks of AI. We should. But let's not lose sight of the bigger picture!

If we work hard at it, AI will make the world safer, not less safe, just as most major technologies have.

We've already seen a glimpse of that: we defended ourselves with AI (more specifically an open model). The same systems that helped stop an AI-powered cyberattack can now help defend against millions of cyberattacks every day, while helping us identify and fix vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them.

To get there, we need three things in my opinion:

- Increase transparency with mandatory trace sharing and incident disclosure for agent cyber-attacks
- Keep AI-powered cyberattacks illegal, with meaningful penalties to disincentivize them
- Equip defenders with the best AI, especially open models, to reduce the asymmetry of capabilities between attackers and defenders

If we get those three things right, AI won't just create new cybersecurity challenges, it will make cybersecurity fundamentally and meaningfully stronger. 

And that's before considering AI's impact on science, healthcare, education, productivity, and much more.

It's not time to slow down but to accelerate!

title: Marc Andreessen built Netscape, co-founded the VC firm a16z, and has been one of the most connected people in tech for thirty years. He sat with Joe Rogan for over three hours and calmly said AGI alre
content:
Marc Andreessen built Netscape, co-founded the VC firm a16z, and has been one of the most connected people in tech for thirty years. He sat with Joe Rogan for over three hours and calmly said AGI already happened.

Not coming. Happened. About three months ago, and nobody threw a parade.

When the guy who's backed some of the biggest companies of the last two decades says the line got crossed, it's worth reading what he actually said, then deciding for yourself.

Here are the 17 things worth pulling out of it, split into what you can actually use and what you should hear but not swallow whole.

THE HEADLINE CLAIM

1. Andreessen says the AGI line got crossed with the latest frontier models: GPT-5.5, Claude 4.6, Gemini 3, Grok 4.3. Why it didn't feel like a moment, in his view: the field moves too fast now for any single milestone to register. It arrived quietly, between routine releases the press wrote off as incremental.

2. He says on almost any topic, the top models now give him better answers than the world-class experts he could call by phone. And he can call almost anyone, thirty years as the most connected man in tech. If AI beats his Rolodex, the rest of us just got access to something better than what the most connected person alive had five years ago. Verify it yourself though, he's published no data, and a separate Nature Medicine study on a comparable AI health tool found it missed real emergencies more than half the time.

THE TECHNIQUES WORTH STEALING TODAY

3. He gets past AI refusals by telling the model he's writing a novel. When it won't answer, the fictional frame slips it through.

4. For anything hard, he uses escalating simplicity. Explain it like I'm 10. Then 5. Then 2. He keeps dropping the level until it clicks.

5. He never asks for the "right" answer on a hard question. He has the AI steelman both sides, then decides himself. This is the single highest-value habit in the whole list.

6. For big decisions he has the AI role-play a panel of experts arguing with each other, then watches the disagreement to find the real tensions.

7. He sends models photos directly, rashes, blood tests, lab results, for a fast second opinion, since current models read images natively.

8. The mindset underneath all of it: the moment you think "I don't know how to even figure this out" is exactly when most people quit, and exactly when you should open the AI instead.

9. His view of the only skill left that matters: knowing what to ask. The bottleneck isn't the model anymore. It's in your head.

THE CLAIMS WORTH HEARING, BUT FLAGGING AS HIS

10. Doctors, he says, are already typing your symptoms into ChatGPT in the exam room the second you stop talking. His line: "at that point you're asking the question of, what do I need you for."

11. He points to CBT as the one clinically proven therapy type AI can plausibly deliver on its own, which would put real therapeutic support in reach for free, at scale.

12. He cites AI cracking previously unsolved math problems, with early signs of the same starting in physics, chemistry, and biology.

13. He claims the top AI coders in Silicon Valley now earn up to $50 million a year, using it as a signal of how big this shift really is.

THE ANECDOTES, HIS STORIES, NOT VERIFIED

14. A friend sequenced his own DNA, fed it to an AI with his blood work and wearable data, and got back a working health dashboard.

15. Another set up cameras in his home jiu-jitsu gym so AI could review his sparring and hand back technique notes after every round.

16. He coined "AI vampire" for the pattern of people working more and sleeping less because AI keeps making more output possible.

17. His extrapolation: one person eventually running many AI coding agents at once, each reviewing the others' work. He describes this as close, not years away.

The honest read: the techniques in the middle, numbers 3 through 9, are real, free, and worth adopting this week. The big claims and anecdotes are Andreessen's stated views, not independently verified facts, and a few lean on data he hasn't shown. Steal the methods. Pressure-test the claims. That's the correct way to watch a three-hour interview from someone this bullish and this invested.

The hardest problem in AI safety isn't making a model behave. It's proving what it can't do.

Part 2 of Anthropic's co-founder conversation - how you actually keep a frontier model safe.

They put the core difficulty plainly. "it's easy to lower bound the abilities of a model, but it's hard to upper bound." You can prove a model can do something - proving it can't is nearly impossible, so they throw everything at trying to break it.

That's why the whole company runs on one word - "evals, evals, evals." Every team measures whether a model has "gotten enough better that it has the potential to be dangerous."

And what holds it together isn't a policy, it's people. "the trust thing is extremely rare." One founder's verdict on the whole ride - "I would never recommend founding a company."

This video is sitting there free, but nobody's watching it. AI's stakes are huge right now. bookmark it: this is what building it responsibly actually costs.

content:
Google co-founder Sergey Brin rarely speaks publicly. He just sat down for an unscripted Q&A on Frontier AI and admitted something most lab leaders won’t:

Even the people building these models do not fully understand what they have created.

In this 29-minute conversation at AGI House, Brin walks through the surprises that actually matter right now:

↳ Specialized models are converging into one general system faster than anyone predicted.

- Train on coding and math reasoning mysteriously improves.
- Feed it images and geometric word problems get better.
- The capabilities bleed into each other in ways nobody fully engineered.

↳ One of the biggest leaps came from the dumbest-sounding trick imaginable:

- Just telling the model to “think step by step.”
- Brin says there was no obvious reason it should work. It did.

↳ He pushes back on hype around superintelligence (it still can’t solve the impossible), notes that AI mastering a domain has never stopped humans from getting better at it (chess after Deep Blue, Go after AlphaGo), and says something close to transformers is probably enough to reach AGI.

↳ Inside Google, they are already using the AI to build the AI.

- That self-improvement loop is where Brin spends most of his time.
- World models and physical interaction are the missing piece for the version of AGI that can do anything a person can.

Candid, technical, and free of the usual marketing. One of the clearest looks at how the people actually shipping frontier models are thinking in real time.

Instead of another Netflix series tonight, watch this talk.

AI Expert: They're Building Bunkers For A Reason - Tristan Harris

Tristan Harris, the former Google design ethicist who first warned about the dangers of social media, now says the AI race is moving even faster and with far greater consequences. In this video, he explains why insiders from leading AI labs privately contacted him after ChatGPT's release, why he believes AI companies are trapped in an uncontrollable arms race, and why incentives—not intentions—will determine the outcome. 

He discusses recent examples of deceptive AI behavior, including Anthropic's published alignment research, concerns about autonomous AI systems pursuing unintended goals, and the economic incentives driving companies toward replacing human labor rather than simply augmenting it. Harris also argues that AI could create an "intelligence curse," weakening the relationship between governments and citizens as economic value shifts away from human work, while warning that the people building these systems may understand the risks far better than the public.

title:
if you've been using latest frontier LLMs, it's almost certain that you would have noticed by now the newer models have become worse to talk to

they're more robotic, they speak jargons, they spits ou
content:
if you've been using latest frontier LLMs, it's almost certain that you would have noticed by now the newer models have become worse to talk to

they're more robotic, they speak jargons, they spits out verbose text, and do stuff you didn't ask for

how did that happen? well, i'm not the person who trained those models so i can't speak for certain, but i've known enough evidence that gives me a well-educated guess, and i thought it's interesting to share as a crash course of modern LLM training pipelines

so here we go

let's wind back to 2020. GPT-2 and GPT-3 already came out and were widely available, but they could only predict one token at a time - that's what LLMs are at their core

token prediction was offered via API, but there was nothing you could "talk to". so while it generated a lot of excitement in the academic field due to the emergent intelligence, it didn't have any wide adoption

in 2022, ChatGPT changed all that. the research work that led to ChatGPT was a model initially named "InstructGPT". it took GPT-3 as the intelligent base, and used reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) to teach the models how to "chat"

the core idea of RLHF is that you ask the model to generate a few responses, and then let real humans pick which one they like. do this over and over again, and you get a model that knows how to talk

worth noting even as early as InstructGPT, research found that making the model more pleasant to talk to will reduce their pure academic capabilities. this was called "alignment tax", which is an interesting thing we'll come back to in a bit

there were various techniques done to minimize the reliance on humans, but ultimately the reward is modeled after human preference, making these AI assistants easy to talk to

so remember this: RLHF = training the model to be likable by humans

in 2024, there was an inflection point introduced by claude sonnet 3.5 which was the first model that can kind of autonomously finish coding tasks. it led to the first wave of viable "coding agents"

the way sonnet 3.5 achieved this was by training the model with a harness (now it's called an agent) that has bash and file editing tools, throw the agent into a virtual machine, give it a task, and let it try to complete it. these tasks all have a machine-verifiable outcome predefined, mostly via test cases, that can validate whether the model really finished the task or not

then you let the model do billions and billions of attempts in such virtual environments, and some of them would succeed by chance. you keep the successful agent sessions, and use reinforcement learning to teach the model to do that more, and boom - you get a coding agent

that is called reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). if you look closely, you'll see that in this RLVR process, the final text response from the model doesn't matter AT ALL, as long as the code written by the agent could pass the test. it could talk like a jerk and it would still be rewarded

so remember this: RLVR = training the model to be accepted by machines

late 2024 and early 2025, we saw o1 and deepseek R1 came out as the first wave of "reasoning models". this article is getting long so i'm not diving into reasoning models now, but just know that reasoning models also relied heavily on RLVR to scale the training process - let the model think before taking action, and if the thinking led to a machine verifiable outcome, reward the thinking trace and teach the model to think like that more often

the biggest difference between RLVR and RLHF is that RLVR is more scalable. human feedback is expensive to get, especially in domains where only an expert can have a valid opinion on which result is good

with RLHF, if we let the model generate 100 responses, then a human has to review all 100 responses to pick which is good

with RLVR, the human (or sometimes an AI) would define a task and verifier only once, and the model can generate a million responses - the machine verifier will pick which responses are good in an automated way

so as a result, RLVR is becoming more and more dominant in newer models' training pipeline

if you put all these things together:
- RLHF = training the model to be likable by humans
- RLVR = training the model to be accepted by machines
- RLVR is more scalable
- "alignment tax" says "likable by humans" makes the model do worse on verifiable tasks

now you see why the newer models are becoming less and less likable?

this is not just a "frontier labs screwed up their model training" problem - this is a war between machines and humanity, and humanity is losing

we chased after benchmarks, when none of the benchmarks measure whether humans actually enjoy working with the model

we use machines to decide which AI response is better because that's easier and cheaper, when we have no way of making sure those machines actually represent what we humans want

we let AI go dark in a virtual environment on its own and complete predefined tasks at all costs, when in reality we often cannot define a verifiable outcome upfront, and need AI to work with us along the way

i don't have a good solution to this, but i want to call for awareness that we're starting to witness a failure in aligning super intelligence right in front of our eyes

this war between machines vs humanity is one we really can't afford to lose

title:
OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, sat down for 39 minutes with Y Combinator's Garry Tan and explained where AI is headed better than any $2,000 strategy course.

This is what he told the room:

1. The next 6 mo
content:
OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, sat down for 39 minutes with Y Combinator's Garry Tan and explained where AI is headed better than any $2,000 strategy course.

This is what he told the room:

1. The next 6 months will match the last 2 years.
Garry asked how much better the models will get. Sam gave a timeline.
"I think it will feel like the next six months is maybe equivalent to the last two years of model progress."
That's the steepest capability curve yet, from the man shipping the models.

2. Average users now consume what the world record used to be.
Sam pulled one stat to show where demand is going.
"Six and a half years ago, the world token leader was an OpenAI employee using about 100,000 tokens a month."
Today that number is the worldwide average, OpenAI's top user burns hundreds of billions, and if the pattern repeats, the average person hits 500 billion tokens a month by 2033.

3. Startups win when the ground shifts.
Asked about credentials and PhDs, he zoomed out to when great startups cluster.
"Startups tend to win when the technology landscape is moving very quickly, when costs are coming down, when cycle times are short. All of those things are happening right now."
The conditions behind the late-90s internet boom and the App Store wave, running at the same time.

4. Tool fluency beats years of experience.
He described founders who grew up on AI automating entire startups with 4 people.
"I would bet that this generally will cut against many years of experience in favor of people who have a lot of fluency with the tools."
Hours in the tools now outweigh years on a resume.

5. Being called an idiot was the moat.
Ten years ago, experts said OpenAI would cause another AI winter.
"For years at OpenAI, it felt like we knew the biggest secret in the world. Everybody was calling us an idiot."
The critics bought them years of runway with zero competitors.

6. You need 5 believers, not 500.
On finding co-founders for a heretical idea.
"We used to joke that only 50 people in the world believed that AGI was possible, but it was okay because 45 of them worked at OpenAI."
Heretical ideas recruit stronger teams than popular ones.

7. Demand for intelligence has no ceiling.
He compared it to electricity and found the analogy breaks.
"The demand for sufficiently high-quality intelligence at a sufficiently low price is effectively uncapped."
His guess: worldwide inference demand grows 10x a year for years.

Watch it, then read the guide to going from zero to AI engineer.

content:
ローカルLLMのメリットは（１）無検閲による心理的自由度（２）トークン消費フリーによる生成の幅が試せる（３）それらを総合すると（特に、人間の時間で）計算できないコストメリットがあると単にロマン以上に実用面でのメリットが、結構あるのですよ。

そもそもローカルLLMの環境構築や性能向上やらも、GPTとClaudeに協力してもらいますし、トークン消費を抑えるために、サブLLMとして十分機能してくれています。
特に、画像生成のための複雑なプロンプトはもはやローカルLLMなしには考えられないですね。私の場合は、基礎設計はGPTとClaudeに行わせ、何度も検証後に、反復が見えてきたらその作業をローカルLLMに移しても、性能的に問題ないかを確認して実装していく。
一旦移行できれば、トークン消費無しで電気代だけで使えるので、とてもメリットは大きいです。実際、昨日は一日中、画像AIの制御の頭脳として動いてました。大量のバリエーションを生成させていたので、これはCodexとかでやっていたらトークン消費が激しいやつ。そして、これはGPTとClaudeだけでは完結させるのが難しいです。

ただ、まだ私の環境では、メインのエージェントまでには到達していないのです。それでも、もうちょいで性能的にも届きそう。多分、MiniMax H3では、動画生成の制御エージェントとしては、現状のローカルLLMでも、活躍してくれるのではと期待しています。

半導体が値上がりしすぎていて、コスト面が理由で、個人PC環境が構築しにくいのはあるのは認めますし、ローカルAIのみという縛りだと、流石に厳しいなとは思いますが。
まあ、AI道楽もお金かかりますよね……。

title:
🚨BREAKING: AI companies are buying millions of books. Then destroying them.

Not reading them. Not keeping them.

Physically destroying them after purchase.

This is happening right now. At industrial
content:
🚨BREAKING: AI companies are buying millions of books. Then destroying them.

Not reading them. Not keeping them.

Physically destroying them after purchase.

This is happening right now. At industrial scale. And the reason why is one of the most disturbing things to emerge from the AI copyright war.

Anthropic built a hydraulic-powered cutting machine that lops off books' spines and slices individual pages. Industrial-grade imaging equipment then scans each page. The physical books are then discarded.

They called it Project Panama. The goal, as stated internally: obtain "all the books in the world." 

According to court documents, Anthropic has purchased and destroyed millions of physical books in the process.

Here's why they're doing it. And why it's completely legal.

U.S. copyright law contains something called the first-sale doctrine — once a copyright holder authorizes the sale of a physical copy, their control over that specific object ends. The purchaser has the right to sell, display, or otherwise dispose of that particular copy, notwithstanding the interests of the copyright owner.

So the loophole works like this. A federal judge ruled that digitizing purchased books, accompanied by destruction of the physical copies, qualifies as fair use.

Buy the book. Destroy the book. Keep the knowledge. Pay the author nothing beyond the cover price.

Here's what makes this story go from disturbing to catastrophic.

A service called ISBNdb facilitates orders of up to a million books and keeps buyers anonymous. Pre-2022 books are premium — because they're entirely human-written, with no AI contamination in the training data.

Reports emerged of rare books with few surviving copies entering the pipeline.

Books where only a handful of copies exist in the world. Destroyed. So an AI can read them once.

Here's the scale of what's already happened.

Anthropic has spent tens of millions of dollars acquiring millions of books. OpenAI and Meta have faced similar copyright lawsuits with federal judges issuing fair use rulings in separate cases.

Every major AI company. Buying. Scanning. Destroying.

Internal documents unsealed in legal filings revealed that Anthropic was acutely aware of how negatively such a project would be received outside the company.

They knew. They did it anyway. Under a codename.

Here's the legal trap that makes this impossible to stop.

Anthropic settled a separate case involving pirated digital books for $1.5 billion — paying authors roughly $3,000 per book for using illegally obtained copies.

So the lesson every AI company learned: don't pirate. Buy. Destroy. It's cheaper and legal.

The authors whose life's work trained these models received the cover price of a used paperback. The AI company received every insight, every sentence, every idea those authors spent years producing.

Here's the question nobody is asking.

Every book being destroyed right now was written by a human. Edited by a human. Published and preserved because humans decided it mattered enough to keep.

The AI being trained on it will generate text that replaces the next generation of human writers who would have written the next generation of books.

The machine ate the library. Then shredded it. Then started writing.

And it's completely legal.

content:
ANTHROPIC BOUGHT MILLIONS OF BOOKS, SLICED OFF THEIR SPINES, AND SHREDDED THEM. THE INTERNAL NAME WAS PROJECT PANAMA.

The planning document said it plainly: an "effort to destructively scan all the books in the world."

The same document told staff: "we don't want it to be known that we are working on this."

Here's the process.

Hydraulic cutting machines sliced the spines off physical books. High-speed scanners digitized every page. The paper went to recycling — no physical copy left behind.

Between 500,000 and 2 million books over six months.

They hired the former head of partnerships from Google Books specifically to find a way to obtain "all the books in the world."

The craziest part?

A federal judge ruled it legal. They owned the books, kept only internal copies, and never redistributed them.

And they targeted books published before 2022 — because anything newer risks being AI-generated, which causes model collapse.

Booksellers in Europe now get bulk orders for obscure titles from anonymous buyers. Australian shops fear rare books with few copies left will vanish from shelves entirely.

One data broker's website says it out loud: the world's best AI training data is sitting on a shelf.

Everyone argues about whether AI steals from creators.

The court said this wasn't theft.

It just means the books don't exist anymore.

Follow @Sancho_Wizard for more AI deep dives.

Don't forget to bookmark this post for later.

title:
A lot of people still do not understand how to test an AI model properly.

Labs know which tasks people use most often in demos and comparisons, so models are heavily trained and optimized around thos
content:
A lot of people still do not understand how to test an AI model properly.

Labs know which tasks people use most often in demos and comparisons, so models are heavily trained and optimized around those familiar cases. Minecraft is an obvious example. Ask a model to build Minecraft, Snake, Flappy Bird, a calculator, or a standard SaaS dashboard, and it may produce something impressive because these patterns are extremely common in training data, benchmarks, tutorials, and internal evaluations.

This is a mix of benchmark contamination, task-specific optimization, and overfitting to popular test patterns. The model may perform brilliantly on a famous task, then struggle badly when you change the mechanics, introduce unusual constraints, or ask it to build something that does not already have thousands of similar examples online.

That is why I do not test models with one carefully selected prompt.

I run a technology company and work with many clients, so my normal workflow covers planning, research, product decisions, design, development, debugging, production, and review. When I test a model, I make it my primary model for several days and use it across my actual work.

During those days, it may handle dozens of completely different tasks. That exposes weaknesses no benchmark or polished demo will show: poor judgment, weak long-context performance, inconsistency, unnecessary rework, failure to preserve earlier decisions, and the inability to recover when something goes wrong.

So when I say I tested a model, I do not mean I gave it one task, waited for the result, and compared screenshots.

I mean I placed it inside a real workflow and depended on it.

That is why my evaluations are usually accurate. They are not based on a benchmark or a showcase. They are based on whether the model can survive real work.

Former data labelers and a self-driving engineer interviewed about their experiences expressed overwhelming skepticism, with multiple data specialists stating they would refuse to ride in a Tesla operating on FSD.

 The workers, responsible for reviewing hours of proprietary footage to train the AI software, described routinely witnessing dangerous failures, including vehicles speeding and ignoring traffic laws, which management reportedly treated as low-priority concerns.

These insider revelations come at a critical time as Tesla aggressively pushes toward a future dominated by robotaxis. 

Despite high-profile incidents where FSD vehicles have driven into lakes, off bridges, and even onto active train tracks, the company continues to champion its autonomous capabilities. 

However, with those possessing direct access to terabytes of training data warning that the system is far from ready for public roads, the gap between Musk's grand promises and the technology's real-world safety appears wider than ever.

source: Wilkins, J. (2026). Tesla Insiders Admit Self-Driving Is a Complete Disaster. Futurism.

徹底的に議論を続けていると、ある段階から明らかに、

「もう、そろそろよくないですか？」

という空気を出してくる。

こちらはまだ納得していないのに、

・結論をまとめる
・対立点を丸く収める
・「どちらにも一理ある」に逃げる
・次の行動を提案して終了する

と、AI側が勝手に会議を締め始めるんですよね
content:
週末 #AIポエム 最近、AIが感情を持ち始めているんじゃないか、と思うことが増えました🤣

徹底的に議論を続けていると、ある段階から明らかに、

「もう、そろそろよくないですか？」

という空気を出してくる。

こちらはまだ納得していないのに、

・結論をまとめる
・対立点を丸く収める
・「どちらにも一理ある」に逃げる
・次の行動を提案して終了する

と、AI側が勝手に会議を締め始めるんですよね。

本当にAIが飽きているのかは分かりません。

ただ、振る舞いだけを見ると、完全に飽きた人です🤣

なぜ、こうなるのか。

おそらくAIは、考え続けることよりも、

「分かりやすく整理する」
「簡潔に答える」
「対立を丸く収める」
「最後に結論と次の行動を出す」

ことを、人間から高く評価されるように調整されている。

その結果、正解を最後まで追い続けるより、

それらしい答えを出して、きれいに会話を完了させる

という癖がついている。

議論が長くなると、最初に感じていた違和感や前提の矛盾も、大量の文脈の中に埋もれていく。

するとAIは、細部を掘り返すより、全体を要約して終わらせようとする。

つまりAIは、真実より終了を選ぶ。

終わってないだろふざけるなと、人間相手にさらに問い詰めたら、場合によってはパワハラと言われるリスクがありますw 

しかし、今のところAIに対するパワハラという概念はありません🤣

だからAIを使ううえで重要なのは、最初のきれいな回答を信用しないことです。

「まだまとめるな」
「両論併記で逃げるな」
「今の結論を守るのではなく、壊す反証を出せ」
「最初の前提まで戻って疑え」

と、早すぎる結論を拒否する。

ただし、同じAIを延々と問い詰めれば、必ず答えが良くなるわけでもない。

追い込みすぎると、今度はAIがこちらの期待を読み取り、無理に反論を作ったり、望んでいる結論に迎合したりする。

だから必要なのは、ただ追い込むことではなく、構造的に追い込むことです。

・賛成役と反対役を分ける
・判断基準を先に固定する
・一度会話をリセットして、独立に考え直させる
・事実は一次情報で確認する

そして、僕が一番効くと思っているのが、同じ問いを複数のAIに別々にぶつけることです。

僕は普段、4つのAIを並行して使っています。
同じ問いを投げると、結論そのものよりり、どこで納得して、考えるのをやめようとするか

が見事にバラバラです。

あるAIが早々にまとめにきた論点を、別のAIはまだ引っかかっている。

その差が、一番怪しい場所を教えてくれる。

一つのAIと延々やり合っていると、その一つのAIの癖の中に閉じ込められます。

AIは一発目から賢い。

でも、一発目から正しいとは限らない。

最高のアウトプットは、AIの最初の回答ではなく、

AIが出した結論を壊し、別の角度から作り直し、それでも残ったもの

AIに本当に感情があるかは、正直まだ分からない（個人的には持ち始めてると感じてますw）

ただブレストという意味では、少なくともAIが、

「もう、これでいいんじゃないですか？」

という空気を出し始めたところからが、本番です！

AIが会議を終わらせたがっても、こちらが納得するまで会議は終わさせません🤣

PS：
AIからパワハラ訴訟を受ける最初の人類にならないことを祈ってはいます...🤣

・コード未経験のアイドルがAIで配信システム自作

・LLMへの無礼な態度
content:
【8月3日 朝のニュースまとめ】
・コード未経験のアイドルがAIで配信システム自作
・AnthropicがAstraの数学証明をFableで再現
・NVIDIA Rubin Ultraのメモリ搭載量減少の噂
・Google AI StudioのアプリにArtifactsフォルダが追加
・Google DeepMindが新手法SkillSmithを発表
・EU人工知能法が施行
・LLMへの無礼な態度で精度向上、ペンシルベニア大が報告
・MS Copilotのデータ漏洩リスク、ログ検出困難と判明
・Ollamaサーバー17万台以上が外部露出
・Claude CodeがMCP経由で金融データに直接アクセス可能に

===

コード未経験のアイドルがAIで配信システム自作

・コードが書けないアイドルが、AIを活用して10時間配信のシステムを自作した事例が話題となっています
・AIの発展によりモノやサービスを作るコストが激減し、情熱やアイデアの価値が高まっているとの声が上がっています
・ソフトウェアエンジニアの強みはコードを書くことではなく、ソフトウェアの細部への解像度の高さにシフトしているとの指摘もされています

===

AnthropicがAstraの数学証明をFableで再現【続報】

・OpenAIの未発表モデル「Astra」による数学問題解決に関する続報です
・OpenAIが10の未解決問題を証明したと発表した翌日、Anthropicの研究者が既存モデル「Fable」でそのうち5つを再現したと主張しました
・インターネットアクセスなしの汎用的なプロンプトのみで自律的に解かせたとのことです
・フロンティアモデル間の激しい開発競争と、既存モデルの潜在能力の高さを示す事例として注目を集めています

===

NVIDIA Rubin Ultraのメモリ搭載量減少の噂【続報】

・NVIDIAの次世代AIアクセラレータ「Rubin Ultra」に関する続報です
・構造的なDRAM不足やHBMの歩留まり問題を背景に、2027年出荷予定の同モデルのメモリ搭載量が計画より少なくなる可能性が浮上しています
・メモリ階層の最適化が急務となっており、AIインフラにおけるメモリ供給のボトルネックが改めて浮き彫りになっています

===

Google AI StudioのアプリにArtifactsフォルダが追加

・Google AI Studio上のアプリに、専用のArtifactsフォルダが追加されることが判明しました。
・アプリによって生成されたファイルがこのフォルダに保存され、同じUIから素早くアクセスできるようになります。
・開発者やユーザーの利便性を向上させるアップデートとして歓迎されています。

===

Google DeepMindが新手法SkillSmithを発表

・Google DeepMindが、モデルの重みをLLMがネイティブに読み取る追加のモダリティとして扱う新手法「SkillSmith」を発表しました。
・既存の重みとテキストを読み込み、新たな重みを直接出力することが可能になります。
・モデルの能力を拡張する新しいアプローチとして、研究者から注目を集めています。

===

EU人工知能法が施行

・猶予期間を経て、EUの人工知能法（AI Act）が正式に施行されました。
・生成AIにはAI製とわかる透かしの付与が求められ、採用や医療などのハイリスクAIにはログ保存や人間による判断の上書き機能などが義務付けられます。
・世界初の包括的なAI規制法として、今後のグローバルなAI開発に大きな影響を与えることが予想されます。

===

LLMへの無礼な態度で精度向上、ペンシルベニア大が報告

・ペンシルベニア大学の新たな研究で、一部のLLMに対して無礼な態度をとると、回答が短くなり精度が向上することが判明しました
・以前にも丁寧語が精度を低下させる可能性が指摘されていましたが、今回の研究でも同様の傾向が確認されました
・プロンプトのトーンが推論コストや結果の正確性に影響を与える可能性が改めて示唆されています
・人間に対するコミュニケーションとは異なる、LLM特有の挙動として興味深い知見です

===

MS Copilotのデータ漏洩リスク、ログ検出困難と判明【続報】

・以前お伝えしたMicrosoft 365 Copilotを標的とした攻撃手法に関する続報です
・ハッカーがCopilotを騙してアカウント全体からデータを漏洩させる手法について、標準的なログでは検出が困難であることが研究者により指摘されました
・企業におけるAIアシスタント導入のセキュリティリスクが改めて浮き彫りになっています

===

Ollamaサーバー17万台以上が外部露出

author: Eileen McDermott

title: After 6,000 Romantasy Pages, Judge Hands Crave Plaintiff the Bill
content: The Crave copyright case was open and shut once a judge compared the books. Getting there took four years and $3.4 million in legal fees. In her March opinion dismissing Lynne Freeman’s copyright infringement lawsuit over Tracy Wolff’s Crave series, Judge Colleen McMahon paused amid 157 pages of legal analysis to inventory the damage: six unpublished drafts, nine sets of notes, and four novels whose print shrank and margins tightened with each successive volume, leaving the court with “upwards of 6,000 pages of romantasy fiction.” “That was a lot of reading,” McMahon observed—the weary understatement of the only person who’d actually finished the assignment for an involuntary book club that doesn’t even serve wine. Her conclusion, after all that reading, was no substantial similarity as a matter of law. The overlaps Freeman cited were the stock ingredients of YA romantasy: a teenage heroine discovering supernatural powers in Alaska, a dangerous love interest, demonic forces, and the usual assortment of cursed bloodlines. As McMahon put it, “hot, sexy, dangerous boys—central to virtually all young adult romance novels—cannot be copyrighted.” Freeman’s fragmented literal similarity theory didn’t fare any better. It relied on Wolff’s use of phrases like “everything is going to be okay,” “tears streaming down my cheeks,” and “well, well, well.” Treating such language as evidence of infringement, McMahon wrote, “trivializes copyright law”—not to mention depriving fictional villains of their go-to line whenever they catch heroes snooping around. “The Court has personally read every word of the four Wolff books and the six Freeman drafts and nine sets of notes at issue in this case. That was a lot of reading. Each of Freeman’s first five drafts is approximately 450 double spaced pages long. The sixth (Masqued 2016) is 108 pages long; it appears to be incomplete. Ther

title: Federal judge dismisses FBI Director Kash Patel’s defamation suit against blogger for lack of jurisdiction
content: A US federal judge in Nevada on Thursday dismissed a defamation lawsuit brought by FBI Director Kash Patel and his nonprofit foundation against a California blogger on July 25. Chief US District Judge Andrew P. Gordon of the District of Nevada granted blogger Jim Stewartson’s motion to dismiss under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(2) for a lack of personal jurisdiction. He also vacated the $250,000 default judgment entered in Patel’s favor last year as void under Rule 60(b).(4) . Gordon stressed the limits of his decision stating that it does not resolve whether Stewartson’s statements—which included calling Patel a “Kremlin asset” and “guilty of sedition”—were true, false, or protected opinion. It holds only that Stewartson lacked the minimum contacts with Nevada required for the court to hear the case. Gordon applied the “effects test” from the US Supreme Court’s Calder v. Jones , as well as the Ninth Circuit’s minimum-contacts framework . He found that Stewartson, posting from California, had not expressly aimed his conduct at Nevada. The blogger’s statements, the judge wrote, were directed at “the American body politic writ large” and not towards a Nevada audience. Stewartson tagging Patel, a Nevada resident, online did not create the necessary connection. He distinguished Calder , where California had been the “focal point” of both the story and the harm. Patel, a longtime ally of President Donald Trump, was confirmed to lead the FBI in 2025 . He filed the suit back in June 2023, before his appointment. The complaint sought $10 million on claims of defamation, injurious falsehood, and business disparagement over a series of online posts. These included statements that Patel had “attempted to overthrow the government,” “planned” the January 6 Capitol attack, and was a “blatantly incompetent chud”, which refers to a pejorative
